## Summary

-   A compute policy lets users create their own compute, but only within the rules you set.
-   Allowlist `data_security_mode` so every new cluster uses a Unity Catalog access mode: Auto, Standard, or Dedicated.
-   Don't block old runtimes one by one. Use an anchored `regex` that sets a minimum version, and new old versions can't slip past it.
-   A policy governs new and edited compute only. Users with unrestricted cluster creation skip it, and existing clusters stay as they are until you enforce compliance.

## The problem

You want every cluster in the workspace to be Unity Catalog compute. That means no
`No isolation shared` clusters and no runtimes too old to talk to Unity Catalog.

You could take compute creation away from everyone and build clusters on request. That
doesn't scale, and it makes the platform team a bottleneck for every notebook.

Use a compute policy instead. Users still create their own compute, but the policy limits
what they can pick. Anything outside the rules can't be created.

## Before you begin

-   You need the Premium plan and workspace admin rights.
-   Create the policy in **Compute > Policies > Create policy**. Paste the JSON under
    **Advanced options > Edit definition as JSON**.
-   Grant the policy's `CAN_USE` permission to the groups that should create compute with it.

## The starting point

A common first draft has two rules. One allowlists the Unity Catalog access modes. The other
blocklists the 10.4 LTS runtimes:

``` json
{
  "data_security_mode": {
    "type": "allowlist",
    "values": [
      "DATA_SECURITY_MODE_AUTO",
      "DATA_SECURITY_MODE_DEDICATED",
      "DATA_SECURITY_MODE_STANDARD"
    ],
    "defaultValue": "DATA_SECURITY_MODE_AUTO"
  },
  "spark_version": {
    "type": "blocklist",
    "values": [
      "10.4.x-cpu-ml-scala2.12",
      "10.4.x-gpu-ml-scala2.12",
      "10.4.x-scala2.12"
    ],
    "defaultValue": "auto:latest-lts"
  }
}
```

The `data_security_mode` rule is sound. An allowlist names the only values a user can pick,
so `NONE` and the legacy passthrough modes are gone.

The `spark_version` rule has two gaps.

**It blocks keys, not labels.** The runtime dropdown shows `10.4 LTS (Scala 2.12, Spark 3.2.1)`.
The policy only sees the API key, `10.4.x-scala2.12`. If you paste the display names into a
blocklist, the policy saves but blocks nothing. List the real keys with
`databricks clusters spark-versions`.

**It blocks exactly three strings.** The docs say a blocklist needs exact matches. Every
runtime not on the list is allowed, including 9.1 LTS, 7.3 LTS, and any other 10.4 key, such
as a Photon build. A blocklist of runtimes also gets out of date. Each time a version reaches
end of support, someone has to remember to add it.

## Set a floor, not a blocklist

Flip the rule round. Say which runtimes are allowed, and let everything else fail:

``` json
{
  "data_security_mode": {
    "type": "allowlist",
    "values": [
      "DATA_SECURITY_MODE_AUTO",
      "DATA_SECURITY_MODE_STANDARD",
      "DATA_SECURITY_MODE_DEDICATED",
      "USER_ISOLATION",
      "SINGLE_USER"
    ],
    "defaultValue": "DATA_SECURITY_MODE_AUTO"
  },
  "spark_version": {
    "type": "regex",
    "pattern": "^(auto:.*|(1[5-9]|[2-9][0-9])\\..*)$",
    "defaultValue": "auto:latest-lts"
  }
}
```

The regex accepts:

| Value | Example | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `auto:` special values | `auto:latest-lts` | These always point at a supported runtime |
| Major version 15 to 99 | `15.4.x-scala2.12`, `17.3.x-scala2.13` | Sets a floor at 15 that newer releases clear on their own |

It rejects `14.3.x-scala2.12`, `10.4.x-photon-scala2.12`, and `9.1.x-scala2.12`. It does this
without naming any of them.

Why 15, not 14.3 LTS? 14.3 LTS goes out of support on 1 February 2027. A floor at 15 saves you
editing the policy again in three months. Pick the floor that suits your estate. Raise it by
changing one number.

::: {.callout-tip title="Anchor the pattern" appearance="simple"}
The docs say to anchor a regex at both ends. Without `^` and `$`, a pattern like
`1[5-9]\..*` would also match inside other strings. Write the anchors yourself and the
policy behaves the same whatever the engine does.
:::

The access mode allowlist also includes the legacy names. `USER_ISOLATION` is the old API
name for Standard and `SINGLE_USER` is the old name for Dedicated. An allowlist is an exact
string match. If you list only the new names, older Terraform modules and job definitions
that still send `USER_ISOLATION` can fail the policy, even though they ask for the same mode.

## Watch for

**Auto is not always Standard.** Auto picks Standard unless the user selects an ML runtime,
a GPU instance type, or a runtime below 14.3. Then it picks Dedicated. Both are Unity Catalog
modes, so the policy is still met. But expect some clusters to be Dedicated when you
expected Standard. To require Standard, fix it with `"type": "fixed"`.

**Defaults are UI-only.** `defaultValue` fills in the create compute form. It isn't applied to
compute created through the Clusters API unless the request sets
`apply_policy_default_values: true`. The allowlist and regex still apply either way. API
callers can't break the rules, but they don't get your defaults.

**Unrestricted cluster creation skips the policy.** Users with the
**Unrestricted cluster creation** entitlement see an **Unrestricted** policy and can build
anything. Remove that entitlement from the `users` group, or the policy is only a suggestion.

**Check Personal Compute too.** By default every user can use the **Personal Compute**
policy. Your new policy doesn't close that route. Either restrict who can use Personal
Compute, or override its family rules with the same `spark_version` floor.

**Editing a policy doesn't fix existing clusters.** Clusters created before the change keep
their old config. Open the policy and check the **Compliance** column, or run
**Scan all resources for compliance**. Then use **Enforce all**. For all-purpose compute,
**Enforce on next restart** applies the change without interrupting running work. Job
compute is updated straight away.

**Unpoliced clusters stay unpoliced.** A cluster created with no policy isn't touched by any
of this. Use **Add compute to policy** from the policy page to bring it in. Any running
cluster you select is restarted, and you can't skip the restart.

**Deleting a policy freezes its clusters.** Clusters governed by a deleted policy keep
running, but only users with unrestricted cluster creation can edit them. Clone and fix a
policy rather than delete and recreate it.

**Runtime 19 adds its own rules.** On Standard access mode in Runtime 19 and above, some
Spark configuration keys are blocked, such as `spark.driver.extraJavaOptions` and
`spark.executorEnv.*`. If your policy fixes one of them, clusters on Runtime 19 fail to
create. Clean those keys out of the policy before you raise the floor.
